svg.aria-label: Diagram: what AWS Network Access Analyzer asserts, how a Network Access Scope poses the question, and the two documented bounds on what a result covers. AWS describes Network Access Analyzer as a feature that identifies unintended network access to resources on AWS, used to specify network access requirements and to identify potential network paths that do not meet them. It uses automated reasoning algorithms to analyze the network paths that a packet can take between resources in an AWS network, and produces findings for paths that match a customer defined Network Access Scope. It performs a static analysis of a network configuration, meaning no packets are transmitted in the network as part of the analysis, and because it only considers the state of the network as described in the configuration, packet loss due to transient network interruptions or service failures is not considered. That is the right trade for the question being asked, since a connectivity test reports whether a packet got through at one moment while reasoning over configuration reports whether the configuration permits a packet at all, and the latter does not require the path to have been exercised. Not transmitting packets also means the analysis has no blast radius, with no scan traffic to whitelist and no risk of a probe being mistaken for an intrusion, which matters for a control intended to run against production regularly. The definition of a finding is precise: a Network Access Analyzer finding is a network path that a packet can take in a network. Elsewhere on the same page AWS states that Network Access Analyzer makes a best effort attempt to return a diverse, representative set of findings from among all possible findings. Read together, a finding is positive evidence that a path exists, while the finding set is described as representative rather than complete, so the service is not offering to enumerate every path matching a scope. That distinction matters for how results are used, because running the analyzer, fixing the paths it reported, and seeing a clean next run feels like closure but is not the same as establishing that no paths exist. The second bound on a result is coverage. AWS states that not all AWS network configurations are supported. Network Access Analyzer does not produce network paths through resources associated with Amazon API Gateway, AWS Global Accelerator, Traffic Mirroring, AWS Wavelength, or AWS Direct Connect. It cannot produce network paths containing customer managed Amazon EC2 instances that modify packet forwarding behavior, which covers any self-run forwarding appliance. It supports internet gateways and virtual private gateways at the beginning or end of a path but does not report paths that pass through them, which AWS explains as those resources being outside of AWS networking and therefore out of scope. It does not support NAT reflection at internet gateways, does not support advanced forwarding rules for Application Load Balancers, and does not support nested Resource Groups. The two bounds are independent and both apply to the same clean run, so a scan can miss a path either because it did not enumerate it or because that class of path is not analysed, and neither is a defect. On the structure of the question, a Network Access Scope defines outbound and inbound traffic patterns including sources, destinations, paths and traffic types, and consists of one or more match conditions and zero or more exclusion conditions. The analyzer identifies network paths in the scope that match at least one of the match conditions and none of the exclude conditions, and where a scope has multiple match conditions it produces findings for any path satisfying at least one of them. A match condition defines the types of network paths that should be produced as findings and a scope must specify at least one. So matches form a union and exclusions veto, which makes an exclusion condition the most powerful element of a scope, and the through field is the broadest because a through entry contains exactly one element containing a resource statement and excludes paths that contain the specified network component anywhere along the path, not just at the beginning or end. A through exclusion naming a firewall is precisely how to ask which paths bypass the firewall, which is the intended use, and it is also how a scope can return nothing while paths exist, if the excluded component sits on more of the paths than whoever wrote the scope expected. On supported resources, findings can only start or end at internet gateways, network interfaces, transit gateway attachments, VPC interface endpoints, VPC gateway endpoints, VPC gateway load balancer endpoints, VPC service endpoints, VPC peering connections and virtual private gateways, while a path may pass through a wider set that adds load balancers, NAT gateways, network ACLs, network firewalls, VPC route tables, security groups, target groups and transit gateway route tables. Reading those two lists against each other shows the shape of the question the service answers, since the endpoints are interfaces and gateways while the middle of a path is where the controls live. On the quality of the documentation, a service doing automated reasoning over a large configuration space could describe its output as all paths matching a scope and leave the sampling unstated; this one states it in the overview of how the service works rather than in a limitations appendix, which is what lets a reader calibrate a result rather than over-trust it, and the unsupported list is long, specific and includes items that are not obscure. The recommended practice is to use the analyzer to find things rather than to prove their absence, since a finding is actionable on its own while an empty result is a weaker statement than it appears and the right next question is whether the scope was drawn to match the concern; to write the unsupported list beside the scope definitions and walk the actual topology against it once, since knowing which regions of a network the service is not describing is more useful than any single finding; and to treat the scope itself as an artifact under review, reading its exclusion conditions and asking what fraction of paths they remove before accepting a clean result, because a scope excluding a component that sits on most paths will return few findings for reasons unrelated to security posture.
svg.title: A finding is positive evidence of a path; an empty result is bounded twice over
svg.text: It reasons instead of probing. The answer is strong in one direction only.
AWS Network Access Analyzer — “no packets are transmitted in the network as part of this analysis”.
A FINDING — a strong positive claim
“A Network Access Analyzer finding is a network
path that a packet can take in a network.”
Found by “automated reasoning algorithms” over
configuration — so a path never used still counts.
NO FINDINGS — a much weaker one
“makes a best effort attempt to return a
diverse, representative set of findings from
among all possible findings”
Representative. Not an enumeration.
Two independent bounds, and both apply to the same clean run
COMPLETENESS a representative set from among all possible findings → it may not have enumerated yours
COVERAGE “Not all AWS network configurations are supported” → it may not analyse that class
Neither is a defect. Both are reasons to read an empty result as “nothing surfaced” rather than “nothing exists”.
Out of scope, by design
API Gateway · Global Accelerator · Traffic
Mirroring · Wavelength · Direct Connect
No paths through “customer managed Amazon EC2
instances that modify packet forwarding behavior”.
Also: no transit through gateways, no NAT reflection.
The scope is the question you asked
Matches union: findings for “any path that satisfies
at least one”. Exclusions veto.
A “through” entry excludes paths containing the
component “anywhere along the path”.
Which is how a scope returns nothing while paths exist.
The audit that pays: map what the tool is not describing
Do you run an EC2 instance that forwards packets? Reach anything over Direct Connect, API Gateway, Global Accelerator?
Each yes marks a region of your network outside the answer — worth more than any single finding.
Use it to find things. Not to prove their absence.
Where you need an assertion about absence, the control that produces one is a policy that prevents the configuration,
not a scan that did not report it.
AWS puts both bounds in the page explaining how the service works, not in a limitations appendix. That is what lets you
calibrate a result instead of over-trusting it.
